newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Struggling Belgian builders appeal for help.
newsitem.headline: Struggling Belgian builders appeal for help.

text.p: Belgian builders, struggling in the face of stagnating orders, wafer thin margins and low public spending, appealed on Wednesday for the government to extend a special reduction in value added tax (VAT).

To boost the industry, one of the country's economic heavyweights, the government agreed in January 1996 to reduce the rate of VAT from 21 percent to 12 percent for private home building and to six percent for public housing.
The reduction is due to run out at the end of December this year.

"We insist most strongly that the reduction in VAT is extended to the end of 1998 or even the year 2000," Rob Lenaers, president of the Belgian Building Confederation, told a news conference. "If there is one message from today, that is it."

Lenaers said he realised belt-tightening in order to meet the European Union's Maastricht Treaty single currency criteria curbed public spending and that this was also the reason the government was ending the VAT reduction.
But he said the Confederation had calculated that raising the VAT rate would hit the industry hard and add to unemployment.
Lenaers said 900 of the 3,500 new houses on the order books for this year were directly linked to the 12 percent VAT rate, involving more than 2,600 jobs.
The negative budgetary impact of maintaining the reduced VAT rate would be neutralised as soon as 1,200 houses had been built, he said.

The Belgian construction sector turns over close to 1,000 billion francs a year, is the biggest employer of manual workers with close to 170,000 on the books and in total produces work for some 225,000 people.
